item.title: Big Tech and authoritarian states: Belarus
item.dc:creator: Daria Dergacheva
item.description: In the latest GV podcast, we discussed why Russia restricts access to many social media services, while Belarus does not impose comparable restrictions; censorship, surveillance, and digital authoritarianism — Belarusian style.
item.content:encoded:
A Global Voices video podcast on the state of digital repression in Belarus

Originally published on Global Voices

Interviewer: Daria Dergacheva | Guest: Mikhail Doroshevich.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

There are more autocracies in the world in 2026 than there are democracies. Some researchers identify digital authoritarianism as the use of digital technology by regimes to surveil, repress, and manipulate domestic and foreign populations. Others argue that the same practices are also carried out by hybrid and democratic regimes. However, they can not execute them without major tech companies becoming complicit, with or without their knowledge. 

Typically, when speaking about digital authoritarianism, academics and media talk about China and Russia (and occasionally Iran and Syria).  However, countries such as Belarus (or Eritrea, Nicaragua, Afghanistan, Myanmar) that consistently rank as more authoritarian than China are rarely discussed.

Global Voices invited an expert on Belarusian internet, digital rights and media, Mikhail Doroshevich, on the GV video podcast “Big Tech and Authoritarian States.”  We discussed why Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenka’s regime is not blocking Western social media platforms, how the internet and self-censorship are weaponized, and how platforms help the regime to spread its propaganda. 

You can view and listen to the podcast in Russian on our YouTube Channel and read the translated transcript below:

Daria Dergacheva (DD): Hello, dear viewers. My name is Daria Dergacheva, and welcome to another Global Voices video podcast. Today we are discussing Big Tech and authoritarian states. Our guest is Mikhail Doroshevich, who works on digital issues in Belarus. We will speak in Russian, but an English translation and subtitles will be available. Please leave your questions in the comments and like the video.

Mikhail, welcome. Please tell us a little about yourself. This is the second Global Voices video podcast I have hosted, and today we want to focus on Belarus.

Mikhail Doroshevich (MD): I can describe myself very briefly, in one sentence: I am a researcher who has been studying the Belarusian internet for more than 30 years. A well-known political scientist once introduced me in a publication as a “veteran of the Belarusian internet.” Since then, I have jokingly used that description myself. But let us talk about something more interesting.

DD: Being a veteran of the Belarusian internet is interesting in itself! I would also like to talk about its history and what is happening now. I recently saw an article from Carnegie suggesting that the internet in Belarus remains considerably more open than in Russia. I find this paradox fascinating. How does the Belarusian regime deal with Western, Chinese, and Russian platforms?

MD: That is quite a complicated technical question. In infrastructural terms, the Belarusian internet has always been more restricted than the Russian internet. By infrastructure, I mean connectivity and connections to the global internet. Since the 1990s, Russian internet providers and mobile telecommunications companies have had their own international connections. Belarus, by contrast, has always had a vulnerable infrastructure.

International connections were controlled by state-owned companies, including the national operator. Private providers and mobile operators never had their own independent international connections. Yet today Russia restricts access to many social media services, from LinkedIn onwards, while Belarus does not impose comparable restrictions on those platforms. So Belarus historically had greater technical constraints, and shutdowns regularly accompanied political campaigns. Blocking websites and resources designated as extremist or terrorist is still widespread and ongoing. But Belarus has not followed the path Russia has taken in recent years. Their technological approaches have diverged.

DD: Do you think the platforms comply with [blocking or takedown] requests from the Belarusian state? Why is this happening?

MD: We would have to look at the platforms’ annual transparency reports. Of course the state sends requests. As far as I recall, both Meta and Google have reported receiving requests from Belarus. Whether and how they respond is another matter. That is a question for the platforms themselves. Belarus also faces restrictions imposed by technology companies. For example, some artificial intelligence services are unavailable to Belarusian users.

DD: And ChatGPT?

MD: That is OpenAI. Yes, OpenAI’s services are unavailable.

DD: In April, YouTube removed Belarusian television channels that had previously been available. Has anything changed since then, or do they remain removed? And why did the government apparently not react?

MD: The government did react. Additional channels were affected in September, with one taken down literally during a live broadcast. It is important to understand that YouTube does not simply switch a channel off without a process. It has a three-strikes system, and these channels had received strikes. They knew about them, not least because they were creating alternative channels. They tried to move their content and audiences to alternatives both in April and in September. The September ban suggests that the enforcement was connected to ownership rather than only to content. Our hypothesis about the April removals was that they were content-related: The television channels’ YouTube accounts probably violated several platform rules. Strikes can be contested after a period of time, but that involves a legal or formal procedure.

DD: So the government has not restricted YouTube in retaliation for the removal of state-media channels?

MD: No. Many other state-owned Belarusian media outlets continue to operate on YouTube and upload hundreds of videos each month. Some of the channels that were removed are trying to move their content to Rutube [a Russian video platform]. Belarus also has a domestic video platform, but neither comes close to YouTube in technical capabilities, functionality, or usage.

DD: Why do you think Lukashenko’s government has not entered into the same direct confrontation with platforms as Putin’s government? Why does it not block Western platforms? And Russian platforms such as VKontakte still work, correct?

MD: Of course they do. The authorities themselves use these platforms. That brings us back to the previous question: Why block the platforms on which they operate?

DD: Have Google or Meta services blocked state-supported media or other accounts associated with the Belarusian authorities?

MD: There have been removals following user complaints, affecting both state and independent media, but only for short periods.

DD: So there have been no major conflicts with Western, Russian, or Chinese platforms?

MD: I doubt that Chinese domestic platforms are widely used in Belarus, apart from among Chinese citizens living there. TikTok is a different case: it is not available inside China itself.

DD: Are people in Belarus punished for posts, likes, and similar activity?

MD: Yes, and it is terrible. Large numbers of people are continually subjected to repression for likes or comments. They receive actual prison sentences and fines. Unfortunately, the practice continues.

DD: Which social networks provide the information used in these cases? Are people punished for activity on Instagram, Facebook, or YouTube?

MD: Yes, absolutely.

DD: Where do the authorities get information about users?

MD: They use, for example, Russian tools for social profiling.

DD: So you believe this is external monitoring?

MD: I do not think the platforms are doing the monitoring. The authorities monitor users themselves, identify them, and punish them. People are also punished for subscriptions to channels discovered during searches of their devices.

DD: For example, subscribing to NEXTA [a progressive, exiled Russian-language media site] could lead to punishment?

MD: Certainly.

DD: What sort of sentences do people receive?

MD: They can be enormous and appalling. Even a minimum sentence would be a deeply troubling precedent in itself.

DD: So people practice self-censorship: they avoid liking, reposting, or writing things?

MD: Of course. It is a matter of personal safety and, unfortunately, part of everyday life in Belarus. But it is important to understand that avoiding these activities does not necessarily make people safer. Nor does it improve national security. What increases is repression. The costs of these measures are unjustifiable: they do not make life in Belarus safer or more peaceful.

If there were some sort of social contract in which restrictions led to fewer crimes or greater security, that would at least be an argument. But that is not what happens. People face severe financial penalties and restrictions for likes and reposts. You know how these platforms work: someone can accidentally like something while scrolling. People of all ages are affected, from young people to the elderly. Older users may be especially vulnerable to accidental interactions. And if we look at online fraud and other cybercrime, even official statistics show that these problems are not decreasing.

Restricting access to information resources does not reduce cybercrime. Preventive measures, media literacy, and education would do much more to protect people from criminals. Those would be more important and meaningful goals.

DD: As far as I know, Russia actively uses social media platforms, including Western ones, to spread disinformation or propaganda, whichever term you prefer. Does Belarus do the same?

MD: If Belarusian state actors are active on these platforms, then, as you can imagine, they do.

DD: Do you mean through official accounts, or also through trolls?

MD: There is an important distinction here. State news agencies and state-owned media generally observe certain boundaries in their written website publications, even when they present events in a particular way. You do not usually see direct hate speech or doxxing in those articles.

Unfortunately, television material is different. The proportion of such content is much higher in videos than in official written publications. So the same outlet might have a relatively restrained website, with its own preferred formulations, while its YouTube channel contains doxxing, hate speech, and other unacceptable material.

Then there is a third layer: individual, highly toxic channels, which are not meaningfully restricted and can behave much more aggressively.

DD: Do you mean individual propagandists, like those in Russia? Are they mostly funded by the state?

MD: They presumably receive their salaries from their state-owned employers. Whether they make these videos during working hours is something we do not know. But they certainly do not hold back in their language.

DD: What technologies are used to monitor people, including facial recognition and internet surveillance? Are they Western, Chinese, Russian, or domestically developed?

MD: I cannot tell you the exact manufacturers or versions of the software being used. More technically informed specialists would need to answer that. But we regularly see cases in which software developed in democratic countries, not only authoritarian ones, ends up being used in such systems. Unfortunately, when funding is available, companies enter tenders, and the products that meet the purchaser’s requirements are selected and deployed.

DD: Could this be investigated through publicly available procurement information?

MD: I do not follow Belarusian procurement tenders for facial recognition or monitoring systems. That is a separate specialization. There is also a conceptual problem: If a system uses TCP/IP, does that make it Western, Chinese, or Russian technology? TCP/IP itself was not developed in Russia or China.

DD: I know, for example, that many cameras in Moscow are Chinese, and Huawei servers are widely used in some parts of the infrastructure.

MD: That distinction is tricky. Look at where your phone was manufactured. Even if its brand is not associated with China, the device may have been made there.

DD: Of course. In the European Union, there are restrictions on using equipment from certain Chinese companies. I do not know the precise situation in the United States or Canada.

MD: Yes, Belarusian mobile operators use such equipment, and that is a significant issue. There is a similar problem with access to AI models. When Belarusians cannot use certain services, they may turn to Chinese or Russian models, which are censored and limited in various ways. One positive exception is Google’s Gemini, which is available in Belarus.

DD: What about Llama? It is open source.

MD: Yes, but there are questions about its capabilities. We return again to education and skills. People need to know how to use and maintain these models. Open source does not mean free to operate. Running and maintaining a model can be more expensive than simply using a proprietary service.

DD: Remind me why OpenAI and Anthropic do not operate in Belarus. Is it a matter of company policy?

MD: Possibly. There are also sanctions. TikTok, for instance, has imposed restrictions on its Russian operations since 2022, and Belarusian accounts have been used to get around those restrictions. Other social networks do not impose the same restrictions on Russian users as TikTok does.

DD: I have two more questions. Belarus used to have a rapidly developing IT sector, and the government supported some of that growth. What is happening now? Are companies still developing technology, or has everyone left? Does Belarus have its own data centers? Are Russian or Western data centers used? Can Belarusian citizens’ data be stored abroad? And are there domestic AI developments, perhaps based on open-source models?

MD: Let me start at the end. Yes, there is development based on open-source models. As for data storage, the relevant data must be kept in data centers certified by the Operational and Analytical Center, which means in Belarus. The country certainly has its own data centers.

DD: And how is the IT sector doing overall?

MD: It is developing. With the rise of AI, the entire sector worldwide is undergoing a transformation. As for companies that remain in Belarus, their customers are predominantly in the Russian Federation.

DD: Does that mean they also work for Russian military organizations?

MD: We cannot know that without looking at particular companies. It is more a question for specialists familiar with Russia’s infrastructure. Hypothetically, the Russian military might itself face restrictions on contracting developers even from countries such as Kazakhstan, Belarus, or other former Soviet states. So I would not assume that the Russian army uses Belarusian developments. But customers are not only military organizations. And many companies have offices in several countries while still employing hundreds or thousands of people in Belarus. They may be global companies with substantial Belarusian operations.

DD: Thank you very much. We will publish an English transcript of this interview on our website, and the video will be available on YouTube. Thank you again for your time. I hope we will see each other again.

MD: Thank you for your work. It is genuinely impressive. I enjoy reading the material Global Voices produces; it is very interesting.

Written by Daria Dergacheva

item.title: In Brazil’s elections, big techs’ transparency and cooperation policies translate as governance washing, according to this expert
item.dc:creator: Fernanda Canofre
item.description: “Under normal conditions, this is already serious enough, because the platform rules over the information flow in a society, but when you apply it to an electoral dispute, it's even more serious.”
item.content:encoded:
Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University NetLab has been following closely how this election unfolds on social media

Originally published on Global Voices

Art by Global Voices, created in Canva Pro.

Amid a series of corruption scandals, the 2026 general election in Brazil is also flooded with headlines about social media companies’ role in the campaign. Users supporting the candidacy of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the incumbent center-left candidate running for re-election, have been reporting a sudden drop in their Instagram Stories views when posting about politics. They say that Meta AI refused to generate images featuring Lula’s name and party number, while delivering the same request for Flávio Bolsonaro, his far-right opponent and the son of the imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro.

On October 16, Meta admitted technical problems on its platforms which affected how pro-Lula content was delivered to users. As reported by the Associated Press, despite acknowledging “global technical glitches, strict anti-fraud measures, and regulatory compliance rather than targeted suppression,” the company that owns Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook denied any political bias.

Lula filed a complaint against Meta accusing the company of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favor Bolsonaro in the run-up to the election, with a judge from the country’s top electoral court ruling that Meta must adopt measures to ensure equal treatment.

With an estimated population of 214 million, Brazil is an important market for social media platforms. It ranks as the second country by number of WhatsApp users and saw the internet become a key component of Jair Bolsonaro’s ascent around 10 years ago.

To understand the current election scenario, Global Voices spoke to Nicole Sanchotene, project coordinator at NetLab, a research laboratory at Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University (UFRJ) that has been publishing reports on the impact of big tech on the electoral campaign. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Global Voices: What have you identified in NetLab’s recent reports about the elections?

Nicole Sanchotene: É muito difícil avaliar o impacto e os possíveis efeitos para a disputa eleitoral e para a percepção das pessoas. O problema central que a gente tem apontado é sobre transparência, uma certa normalização de possíveis ilícitos eleitorais, pontos que são consenso na resolução do TSE (Tribunal Superior Eleitoral) e não estamos vendo cumprimento pleno das plataformas.

O Kwai, que é uma plataforma com ampla adesão no Brasil, tem mais de 60 milhões de usuários, é bastante usado pelas classes C e D, fez uma parceria com o TSE e não está adequado. Não atende a requisitos básicos, a biblioteca de anúncios político-eleitorais tem falhas no tipo de dado que entrega. A gente tem chamado essas práticas de transparência de fachada.

Cada uma das plataformas tem um problema específico. Seja por dados incompletos, seja pela veiculação ou recomendação de conteúdo que não deveria ser recomendado. O que a gente vê é que elas não estão respeitando plenamente o que é exigido pelas normas brasileiras para garantir um mínimo de condições de igualdade para os candidatos, condições que permitam um ambiente de informação, de propaganda, seguro para os usuários e para a disputa eleitoral.

Nicole Sanchotene: It’s hard to evaluate the impact and possible effects on the running and on people’s perception. The central issue that we’ve been pointing to is transparency, a certain normalization of possible illicit electoral practices, issues that were agreed upon in the TSE [Superior Electoral Court, Brazil's top electoral court] resolution, and we are not seeing the platforms comply fully.

Kwai, a platform with widespread adoption in Brazil, with over 60 million users and largely used by “C and D classes” [lower income groups and the basis of the socio-economic pyramid], partnered with the electoral court, and it’s not suitable yet. It doesn't meet basic requirements; their library for political-electoral ads has flaws in the data delivered. We have been calling this a ‘façade of transparency.’

Each platform has a specific issue. Incomplete data, the publishing or recommendation of content that shouldn't be recommended. What we are seeing is that they are not fully abiding by Brazilian norms to guarantee minimum conditions of equality for the candidates, nor conditions that allow an information and publicty environment safe for users and the electoral running itself.

GV: How important are such platforms in Brazilians’ daily lives?

NS: Tem um relatório da Reuters que mostra como as pessoas se informam cada vez mais pelas redes sociais, por plataformas como YouTube, Instagram. O WhatsApp é uma fonte onde as pessoas recebem informações de pessoas próximas, e elas tendem a confiar em pessoas próximas. O Brasil é um dos grandes mercados do WhatsApp, diversas camadas das nossas interações sociais, profissionais passam por ali. A gente não tem condições de falar de disputa eleitoral sem passar pelas redes sociais e sem passar especificamente pelas plataformas da Meta.

NS: There is a Reuters report that shows how people are getting information more and more from social media, through platforms such as YouTube and Instagram. WhatsApp is a source through which they get information from those who are closer to them, which they tend to trust more. Brazil is a big market for WhatsApp; several layers of our social and professional interactions pass through it. We cannot discuss the electoral dispute without going through social media, especially Meta’s platforms.

GV: People have claimed they noticed a sudden drop in their Instagram stories views after posting about politics, especially if they are leftists. Leandro Demori, a journalist, published screenshots showing his stories fell from an average of one million or 400,000 views to 9,000. Have you been reporting on that?

NS: Não fizemos nenhuma análise em relação a isso. Mas acho que essa discussão tem a ver com a questão da transparência. Não é exclusivo da Meta. Essas plataformas tomam decisões – quanto um anúncio vai custar, que tipo de conteúdo vai aparecer ou não para um determinado usuário, decisões de moderação – em uma grande caixa-preta. Ninguém sabe como elas são tomadas, não existem mecanismos para fiscalizar.

Um argumento que a gente costuma ver com muita frequência é plataformas falando que são intermediárias, empresas de tecnologia, e estão à disposição para serem usadas por quem quiser. E a gente sabe que não é assim. Elas usam os dados dos usuários para recomendar conteúdo e direcionar anúncios, seguindo uma série de decisões editoriais, como uma curadoria, sem possibilidade de escrutínio.

A venda de anúncios para anunciantes, por exemplo, é um sistema completamente opaco. O anunciante compra o anúncio, existe uma promessa de entrega do conteúdo ao usuário, mas ele não sabe efetivamente se esse conteúdo está sendo entregue. E da mesma maneira, nós pesquisadores, jornalistas, o poder público, não temos como saber como essa distribuição de conteúdo é feita.

Os algoritmos são uma grande caixa-preta. A gente consegue fazer alguns testes, mas sempre no nível experimental, porque não existe uma ferramenta que permita isso. Em condições normais, isso já é muito sério, porque a plataforma decide o fluxo de informações numa sociedade, mas quando se aplica a uma disputa eleitoral, tudo fica ainda mais sério. Pode ser que os candidatos estejam concorrendo em condições que não são iguais.

NS: We haven’t analyzed this. But I think it has to do with transparency. It’s not exclusive to Meta. These platforms make decisions — how much an ad is going to cost, what kind of ad will show up or not to a certain user, moderation decisions — in a big black box (flight recorder). No one knows how they are made; there are no mechanisms to oversee it.

An argument we used to hear often is that companies themselves say they are intermediaries, tech companies, available to whoever wants to use them. And we know is not the way it is. They use users’ data to recommend content and direct ads, following a series of editorial criteria, like a curation, without any possibility of scrutiny.

The ads sold to advertisers, for example, are a totally opaque system. The advertiser buys an ad, there is a promise that the content will be delivered to the user, but they don't know if it’s actually being delivered. The same way we researchers, journalists, and public power institutions don’t know how the content is distributed.

Algorithms are also a black box. We can run a few tests, but always on an experimental level, because there isn't a tool that allows it. Under normal conditions, this is already serious enough, because the platform rules over the information flow in a society, but when you apply it to an electoral dispute, it’s even more serious. There is a chance that candidates are running in uneven conditions.

GV: How do you evaluate the electoral justice work in this campaign? Recently, we had a ruling battle to take down and then reinstate a pro-Lula WhatsApp channel. 

NS: O STF [Supremo Tribunal Federal] está no centro do debate sobre as eleições. Alguns ministros que estão no TSE são ministros também do STF, então, a discussão tem sido bastante atravessada por essa disputa de poder dentro dessas instituições. O que a gente tem tentado fazer é entregar dados seguindo o rigor científico.

A gente tem notado que as plataformas têm uma estratégia de política de cooperação e de transparência que funciona quase como um discurso de relações públicas e, na prática, não necessariamente se confirma quando se vai fiscalizar. Existe um discurso, ‘Vamos cooperar, vamos fornecer dados, vamos garantir a isonomia, vamos garantir transparência, vamos garantir o cumprimento das normas,’ e o que a gente vê é que se traduz pouco em algo concreto.

A gente chama isso de transparência de fachada ou de governança de fachada – governance washing.

Por exemplo, nós lançamos um estudo falando sobre anúncios que buscam deslegitimar o processo eleitoral. Vários anúncios que atacavam explicitamente as urnas, falando que as urnas eram fraudulentas, que tinham problemas de software, promovidos por terceiros, em alguns casos por candidatos, e a plataforma simplesmente deixou circular. Porque isso se converte em receita.

São empresas poderosíssimas, do ponto de vista econômico, do ponto de vista político, geopolítico, que têm poder de distribuir, recomendar conteúdo e decidir o que pode e o que não pode, em função dos interesses privados.

NS: The STF [Federal Supreme Court] is at the center of the debate during this election. Some of its justices are also part of the electoral court (TSE), so the discussion has been crossed by the power dispute within these institutions. What we try to do is to deliver facts following a scientific rigor.

We have been noticing that platforms have a cooperation and transparency policy strategy that functions almost like a public relations speech and, in practice, doesn’t necessarily apply once you monitor it. There is a speech: ‘Let’s cooperate, let’s provide data, let’s guarantee isonomy, transparency, the fulfillment of norms,” and what we see is something barely translated into concrete actions.

We call it a façade of transparency or governance — governance washing.

For example, we published a study addressing ads that try to delegitimize the electoral process. Several ads that were explicitly attacking the ballots, saying that there was fraud, software problems, were boosted by third parties, in some cases candidates, and the platform allowed them to circulate. Because it turns into revenue.

These are very powerful companies from an economic, political, and geopolitical point of view, with the power to distribute, recommend content, and decide what is allowed and what is not, according to private interests.

GV: Which takes us to another highly politicized issue in Brazil: the regulation of social media. The far-right calls it censorship, while other groups say it’s necessary. With what we’re seeing in this campaign, does it get another angle?

NS: A decisão do STF pela inconstitucionalidade parcial do artigo 19 do Marco Civil, que até então eximia as plataformas de responsabilidade pelo conteúdo publicado por terceiros, trouxe um novo capítulo para a discussão sobre regulação. As plataformas são hoje passíveis de responsabilização no Brasil pelo conteúdo de terceiros, mas a gente não pode pensar em qualquer tipo de regulamentação, sem falar de transparência.

Tem normas, tem deveres e uma série de condições para que elas possam operar, e nenhuma norma funciona se nós não tivermos mecanismos para garantir que está sendo cumprida. E, em caso de não cumprimento, aplicar algum tipo de sanção ou de banimento.

São empresas privadas tomando decisões de acordo com interesses que conhecemos em parte, mas não sabemos como elas são tomadas, como impactam, se favorecem um lado ou não. Não é censura, proibir conteúdos, nada disso, mas criar regras e colocar essas empresas como parte do debate público, porque elas têm um papel central para o debate público.

Nós fizemos dezenas de estudos sobre anúncios fraudulentos que as plataformas deixam circular – conteúdos com fraude, golpes, que querem roubar dados, dinheiro da população, propaganda enganosa. A ideia é fazer com que normas, leis que existem no mundo offline sejam aplicadas às redes sociais reais, para que os usuários estejam em um ambiente seguro.

O que nós temos visto é que as redes sociais, as plataformas, as big techs, não são capazes hoje de oferecer um ambiente seguro para os usuários e, em caso de contextos eleitorais, como é o caso do Brasil agora, elas não são capazes de garantir condições de transparência, de conformidade com as normas que o Brasil estabelece.

NS: The Supreme Court ruling about the partial unconstitutionality of Marco Civil’s Article 19, which until recently exempted platforms from being accountable for content published by third parties, brought a new chapter to this discussion. Platforms are now liable to be held responsible for third parties’ content in Brazil, but we cannot talk about regulation without transparency.

There are norms, duties, and a series of conditions that must be met for them to operate, and nothing works if we don’t have mechanisms to ensure compliance. And, in case of noncompliance, to apply some form of sanction or ban.

These are companies making decisions based on interests that we only know partially; we don't know how they are taken, their impact, or whether they favor one side or not. It’s not about censorship, forbidding content, nothing like that, but creating rules and placing these companies as part of the public debate, because they have a central role in the public discourse.

We made dozens of studies about fraudulent ads that platforms allowed to circulate — content with fraud, scams, phishing and money-stealing scams, mischievous advertising. The idea is to make norms and laws that already exist in the offline world be applied to social media, so users can have a safe environment.

What we’re seeing is that social media, platforms and big tech, are not capable of offering a safe space for their users and, in case of electoral contexts like Brazil’s now, they are not capable of guaranteeing transparent conditions in conformity with the norms established by Brazil.

GV: And, in a more serious scenario, all these elements that you just pointed out could define an election, change the ruling in a country?

NS: Certamente. Quando nós vemos, por exemplo, gastos de campanhas eleitorais, vemos que as campanhas investem massivamente nas redes sociais. As redes sociais são um termômetro e as orientam enormemente. No portal do TSE, a gente vê esses gastos e estamos falando de cifras de milhões de reais. São investimentos bastante consideráveis.

Um grande divisor de águas foi [o escândalo da] Cambridge Analytica, que usou dados de milhões de usuários para manipular eleições e resultados. Já estamos acumulando quase uma década, de um certo consenso de que parte das eleições se jogam nas redes sociais, que podem sim mudar o voto das pessoas, influenciar. Isso se aplicou durante muitas décadas à mídia de maneira geral, e as redes sociais trazem um grau de sofisticação, de refinamento porque o conteúdo é hiperpersonalizado. O que uma pessoa recebe não é o mesmo que outra de outro perfil. É um grau de refinamento e de capacidade de persuasão capaz de mudar a percepções sobre eleições e candidatos.

NS: Certainly. When we see, for example, the costs of a political campaign, we see that they are investing heavily in social media. Social media is a thermometer guiding campaigns. At the electoral court portal, we can see the money spent, and we are talking about millions of reais [Brazil's currency]. These are considerable amounts.

A great divider was the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which used data from millions of users to manipulate an election result. We’re already reaching almost a decade of a certain consensus that part of the election is played out on social media, which can indeed change people’s votes and influence them. That was applied for many years to media in general, but with social media it gained a certain sophistication, a refinement, since content is hyper-personalized. What a person gets is not the same as another person with a different profile. Such a level of refinement and persuasive capacity is capable of changing perceptions of elections and candidates.

GV: What does this election in Brazil leave as a lesson? 

NS: Vermos plataformas não só como intermediárias, mas como quem decide o que as pessoas vão ver. Elas não são apenas transmissoras de informação, não fazem apenas a mediação. Elas decidem, elas fazem a curadoria, elas usam os nossos dados para isso. E nós não temos a menor ideia de como isso é feito.

Eu acho que a gente precisa ter em mente, a partir dessa eleição e de outras experiências também, que esse é um problema global.

Estamos falando de eleições no Brasil, mas o que a gente vê é a repetição de problemas que já vimos em eleições passadas, com mais ou menos gravidade. São empresas que atuam de maneira global. A maior parte, empresas americanas, que atuam com interesses privados, em alguns casos, abertamente associada ao governo dos Estados Unidos, com relações amplamente reportadas com líderes do governo americano. E não temos nenhum tipo de fiscalização, de transparência, mundialmente, eficaz.

NS: That we can look at platforms not just as intermediaries, but as those who rule over what people will see. They are not merely transmitting information, just mediating. They are making decisions, curating, using our data for it. And we don’t have the slightest idea of how that is done.

I think we need to keep in mind, from this election and other experiences as well, that this is a global issue.

We are talking about the election in Brazil, but what we are seeing is the repetition of issues that we’ve already seen in past elections, with more or less seriousness. These are companies operating globally. Most of them are US companies, acting for private interests, with widely reported links to US government leaders. And we don't have any kind of monitoring or transparency globally that is effective.

Written by Fernanda Canofre

item.title: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, children with Down syndrome are using a video game to safely navigate the internet
item.dc:creator: Nurbek Bekmurzaev
item.description: Being able to use the internet safely is also about being able to participate in everyday life.
item.content:encoded:
A virtual assistant called Sol the Owl guides kids through the game

Originally published on Global Voices

SafeClick is a video game that teaches children with Down syndrome about digital safety. A virtual assistant, Sol the Owl, that guides them through the game. Image by the game's developers, used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement. 

Like their peers, children and young people with Down syndrome are curious about technology and the internet, but there are often no suitable, dedicated tools to help them learn how to safely navigate the web. This is true in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, where children with cognitive disabilities are underserved and tend to end up in digital isolation because of caregivers’ concerns about digital safety and the risks of being online.

There are approximately 550-700 children and adolescents with Down syndrome in the country. They are supported by three specialized associations nationwide: the Association “Life with Down Syndrome of FBiH”, Down Syndrome Association Mostar, and DOWN SY I MI. To teach online safety, these organizations have to rely on online safety tools that heavily feature text, abstract explanations, and complex language, which are not accessible or meaningful for children with Down syndrome.

Stefan Filipovic. Photo used with permission.

A group of developers, IT professionals, and designers in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been working to address the lack of a digital safety tool tailored to children and adolescents with Down syndrome. Their goal is to help young people understand, practice, and feel confident making decisions online.

Global Voices conducted a written interview over email with Stefan Filipovic, a member of this group, to learn how they created a video game to teach children with the genetic condition about digital safety. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Stefan Filipovic (SF): We are a group of IT professionals, developers, and designers from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of our work is in commercial technology, but we also have experience developing educational and socially useful video games, such as Eureka – Edukativna videoigra, an educational game for children, and Lea & Leo, a game about children with diabetes.

We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to use that experience for a group that, in our opinion, is often overlooked when digital products are designed. Young people with intellectual disabilities are using phones and the internet, but many digital tools are simply not designed with their needs in mind.

The video game SafeClick (Siguran klik) allowed us to work on something practical and useful while also learning how to design more inclusively and to involve educators and users in the process.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

SF: While working with Servis Centar “Dajte nam šansu – Zvjezdice” – an association and day center that provides free support to children, young people, and people with developmental disabilities, we saw that young people with Down syndrome were using phones and the internet, but there were very few cyber-safety resources made specifically for them.

Most materials use a lot of text, complicated explanations, or interfaces that are difficult to follow. To our knowledge, parents and educators often end up focusing on limiting internet use rather than teaching young people how to deal with unsafe situations.

We wanted to try something different. With SafeClick, we use simple stories, familiar situations, pictures, and game mechanics to help users practice what to do when they receive a suspicious message, meet someone online, or experience cyberbullying.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

SF: We developed the first playable version of SafeClick. The game is currently awaiting approval by the App Store and Google Play. It is designed for mobile devices, with simple, accessible interactions and visual scenarios.

One important decision was to avoid punishing users for mistakes. Instead, the game explains what happened and gives them another chance. We worked closely with educators and parents and used their feedback to make the scenarios easier to understand.

We are currently in the phase of arranging mentoring sessions with the mentor assigned to us through the project, with the aim of earning additional opportunities to promote the game and  reach as many users as possible.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples. 

SF: Although the game will  be published soon, the initial feedback from special education teachers and parents has been highly practical. Special thanks to Jelena Zilic and her children, who provided the first useful in-game test users’ feedback. They helped us see that situations, which are difficult to explain verbally, can become much easier when they are shown visually and practiced through a game.

For example, instead of simply telling someone not to respond to a stranger online, SafeClick lets them see the message, decide what to do, and practice blocking and reporting that individual, and reporting the situation to a caregiver. I really believe we managed to turn an abstract topic into something young people can actually practice.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed?

SF: Before this project, we mostly thought about accessibility as a product and UX (interface) issue. Working on SafeClick made us look at it differently. Being able to use the internet safely is also about being able to participate in everyday life. Communicate, learn, find information, and be part of your community.

If a person cannot understand or safely use digital services, they are left out. We also learned that privacy and accessibility should not be things added at the end of development. They need to be considered from the beginning. That is something we will take with us into our future projects.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

SF: The biggest lesson for us was that making something technically simple is actually quite difficult. With commercial products, it is easy to keep adding features. With SafeClick, we had to constantly ask ourselves whether a button, animation, sentence, or screen was really necessary.

Our earlier experience with Eureka – Edukativna igra and Lea & Leo helped us understand the value of video games for learning, but SafeClick taught us much more about cognitive accessibility and designing with educators and users in mind.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

SF: Our immediate objective is to publish SafeClick, launch it in the media, and inform the wider community about the game’s availability. Looking ahead, we plan to build on this experience to develop a wider portfolio of digital tools tailored for marginalized groups and to continue exploring how games and other digital tools can make learning and participation easier for people who are often left out of mainstream technology. We are open to new collaborations and partnerships.

Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

item.title: Complementary forces: Why activism needs art to drive action
item.dc:creator: Guest Contributor
item.description: "Artistic activism uses the emotional experience of art as a prompt for action and directs that action towards change, turning a complex problem into a clear public message."
item.content:encoded:
‘A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention.’

Originally published on Global Voices

An urban art piece called “The Post is fast, it's only the letters that arrive slowly” in front of the main Post Office in Skopje, North Macedonia.

This post is by Nikola Pisarev, an art historian and a pioneer of creative activism in North Macedonia, who serves as the program director at the Contemporary Art Center in Skopje. It is also part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

In recent decades, practices that bring art directly into people’s everyday lives have become increasingly common. They may be initiated by artists, activists, informal groups, or citizens who use creative means to draw attention to a problem, express disagreement, or call for change. Public spaces become a place where an action meets an audience, provokes a response, and starts a conversation. This approach, when artistic and creative means are used to press for solutions or encourage social change, is called artistic activism.

The “Monument to Diazepam” raised awareness about overuse of prescription drugs. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.

At their core, art and activism have different but complementary roles. Activism seeks to change a situation through strategic planning and advocacy; art, on the other hand, is not pro or against but can move people emotionally.

Art can change how people see and experience a situation. It opens up new perspectives and associations, and its effects are not always immediate or easy to measure. Artistic activism brings these possibilities together: It uses the emotional experience of art as a prompt for action and directs that action towards change.

Urban art actions in North Macedonia offer local examples for exploring this approach. Many actions were developed through direct engagement with specific problems, rather than as part of a broader methodology. They began with a desire to point out an injustice, raise a question, or help address a problem.

Urban art action “Fishing for Potholes” in Veles, North Macedonia, which included public performance and distribution of photo and video coverage. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.

What makes artistic activism compelling?

It does not always take a large crowd to draw attention to a problem. A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention even when it is created by a small group — or by a single person. This does not replace the power of mass organizing, but it makes action possible when resources are limited.

Additionally, amid the constant barrage of information, an unusual sculpture, a witty message, or an intervention in public space can interrupt people’s routine scrolling. They may photograph and share the action, extending its reach beyond the place where it took place through social media and communication platforms.

Still, a high number of views does not mean the problem has been solved. Visibility is an opportunity that needs to be connected to the action’s purpose.

Within high-risk or authoritarian contexts, creative action can also give activists greater room to act, even under pressure. Humor, metaphor, and unexpected forms can sometimes make a problem visible without direct confrontation. In some cases, the people behind an action can also remain anonymous. This does not make them immune to pressure: The level of risk depends on the context, the subject, and the way the action is carried out. But a creative form may allow organizers to absorb some of that pressure while keeping the affected community less exposed.

Likewise, a problem hidden in reports, procedures, or individual experiences can remain invisible to the larger public. An artistic action can translate a complex situation into an image, object, or scene that people can readily recognize. This can encourage citizens, experts and decision-makers to discuss the problem and possible solutions. The challenge is to make the message clear without distorting the substance of the issue.

Art also has a way of enduring long after it has disappeared from public space. A scene, symbol, or object can become a story that the media and the public continue to share after the intervention has ended.

The people behind an action do not need to specialize in every aspect of the problem. They do need to understand its core, use reliable information, and listen to those directly affected.

There are countless ways artistic activism can affect a community. It might prompt an immediate response from the authorities, change how people see an issue, or encourage other social actors to get involved.

Immediate response and problem-solving

Satirical plaque, supposedly from the Guinness Book of Records for the “World Record for the Longest Road Construction” for an street in Skopje that laid unfinished for years. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.

Some actions prompt the authorities to respond quickly. This most often happens with concrete local infrastructure problems: potholes, broken streetlights, faults in water or electricity networks, and smaller environmental issues.

North Macedonia has seen many examples: “The Guinness World Record for the Longest Road Construction”; rubber ducklings placed in the mud at the entrance to a kindergarten in Štip; “fishing” for potholes in Veles; a celebration of the first birthday of a landslide near Kratovo; and the swan lake protest in Orhid. These actions made the situation visible and helped bring about solutions.

However, street art actions can also address wider issues, such as personal data protection, disinformation threats, or corruption.

Changing views and perceptions

Some problems are treated as untouchable, while expert and activist explanations can struggle to reach a wider public. Artistic activism can bridge that gap through the accessibility of an artwork: A simple, readable form can make serious phenomena and policies easier to grasp, encouraging people to question views they may previously have accepted or failed to notice.

Simple Styrofoam fins simulated sharks in the Vardar River in the center of Skopje, next to buildings in the shape of sailing ships made as part of Skopje 2014 project. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.

Some famous examples of street art activism in North Macedonia include “Sharks in the Vardar River,” which commented on the Skopje 2014 project; “The Eyes of the Trees,” about excessive tree-cutting in Skopje; the “Monument to Diazepam” to raise awareness about overuse of prescription drugs; the Ohrid trout’s speech for St. Nicholas Day; the giant nest carrying a message from birds; and the campaign for the referendum to save GTC, the historic public City Shopping Center in Skopje.

Using different approaches, these actions invited citizens to reconsider their views on public policies and decisions.

Added art warns about the plight of the trees. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.

Encouraging public responses and broader engagement

Some actions aim to provoke responses and mobilize a range of actors. These include not only authorities and institutions, but also professional associations, specialist non-governmental organizations and other groups working on specific issues. At times, such groups may engage less often with the problems citizens face, because communication with communities is limited or because they are reluctant to leave their comfort zones.

The media play an important role in this process. Prompted by an action, they seek answers from different actors. When answers are not forthcoming, pressure grows on those actors to take the problem more seriously. In this way, public attention and media coverage can encourage wider engagement.

A “clean air cabin” ironically offering “fresh mountain air” in the city of Skopje, which suffers from excessive pollution. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission.

Early actions on air pollution in Skopje in 2010 and 2011 are one example. With media support, the group “Urban Art Actions” pressured environmental organizations to take air pollution more seriously.

A similar approach appears in “Bread for All” about poverty; “How Many More Victims?” about cyclist safety in Skopje; and more recent actions on river pollution (featuring a mobile statue of floating feces). In these cases, public pressure helped bring the issues to greater attention among organizations and the wider public.

Some of artistic activism’s effectiveness comes from the way actions are made. Preparation often takes place in a studio or garage. It requires serious effort, but can also be an engaging and creative process. Working this way may help people avoid some of the burnout associated with sustained activism, although it does not remove the pressures that can come with public action.

Another source of artistic activism’s effectiveness — and one reason it is becoming more visible in public communication — is its ability to make a problem difficult to ignore. When that happens, the political cost of inaction can rise. Authorities may begin to view a problem in terms of its potential effect on voters at the next election. If the cost of addressing it is lower than, or comparable to, the possible loss of votes, a response and a solution become more likely.

Written by Guest Contributor

item.title: Independent journalism under siege in Georgia
item.dc:creator: Incubator for Media Education and Development (iMEdD)
item.description: Georgia’s deteriorating press freedom is part of a broader process of democratic backsliding, with the right to peaceful protest severely restricted, opposition politicians jailed, a decline in judicial independence, and more.
item.content:encoded:
Need for a unity became urgent in April 2025, after the law on approval of foreign grants

Originally published on Global Voices

Photo by Slava Taukachou on Unsplash

This article by Elli Kostika is an edited version of a longer piece, first published on June 11, 2026, by the non-profit journalism organization Incubator for Media Education and Development (iMEdD). This excerpt is published on Global Voices, with permission under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license. Any use of images or charts by third parties requires permission.

As Georgia has dropped to 135th place in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, iMEdD spoke with representatives of four independent media outlets about the challenges facing journalism in the country: imprisonments, attacks, “foreign agent” laws, and the struggle for survival.

Tamar Rukhadze, Deputy Director of Georgian outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti, describing the state of Georgia’s press, said:

Ι cannot remember any other period in Georgia’s recent history, since I’ve started as a journalist in 1997, with such a harsh and hostile environment towards journalists, media workers and civil society.

Georgia’s government, led by the Georgian Dream party, has intensified its crackdown on media by adopting a series of restrictive laws aimed at suppressing the country’s independent media. Meanwhile, Georgian journalists have been facing constant threats, from legal challenges to physical attacks.

Georgia’s deteriorating press freedom is part of a broader process of democratic backsliding, with the right to peaceful protest severely restricted, opposition politicians jailed, a decline in judicial independence, and a disputed election in October 2024.

Although Georgia has been an EU candidate country since 2023, the ruling Georgian Dream Party, founded by oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, has pivoted the country’s foreign policy towards Russia. However, large segments of Georgia’s population remain pro-EU, and citizens have been protesting for over 500 consecutive days since November 2024, following the contested October 2024 elections and the government’s decision to suspend efforts to advance Georgia’s EU accession process until 2028. 

As the struggles of Georgia’s independent journalists have intensified in this increasingly repressive environment, so too has their determination to survive.

A CEO behind bars, yet her colleagues press on

Batumelebi and Netgazeti have paid a heavy price for their independence. The outlets’ co-founder and CEO, Mzia Amaglobeli, was arrested on January 12, 2025, after an altercation with a police chief in Batumi, Georgia’s second-largest city. Following a trial which press freedom groups denounced as politically motivated, Amaglobeli has been sentenced to two years in prison. 

In December 2025, the European Parliament awarded her the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought. She remains detained under deplorable conditions. Her eyesight — already poor before her imprisonment — is now almost completely lost, Rukhadze tells us, while her lawyers spent six months securing permission for her to visit a clinic, as medical facilities within the penitentiary system lack proper equipment. 

In an interview with iMEdD, Rukhadze stresses the deep psychological effects Amaglobeli’s sentence has had on the newsrooms. “We aren’t the same as we were earlier before this imprisonment,” adding, “It’s a nightmare for every single journalist to become news.”

Rather than resorting to self-censorship, Batumelebi’s and Netgazeti’s journalists have persisted in their reporting. She highlights:

The first thing Mzia did after her arrest was to send a message from prison, asking her team to continue their work as before — to do what they had always done and what they are known for: professional, ethical watchdog journalism that gives a voice to those who need it most.

Weaponizing the law

Arrests and detainments are only one of the ways the Georgian government uses legislation against the country’s independent media. Nino Bakradze, co-founder and editor-in-chief of iFact, tells iMEdD they have lost 90 percent of their income since May 2025 owing to a series of laws that have restricted the outlet’s access to foreign funding.

Georgian media, civil society organizations, and individuals receiving financial support from abroad are obligated to register as foreign agents under the 2025 Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) and face criminal liability for noncompliance. When such provisions are combined with the 2025 amendments to the law on grants, which require foreign donors to obtain governmental approval before offering grants to Georgian recipients, the causes for iFact’s financial troubles become clear.

Because foreign grants had been a major source of funding for Georgia’s online media for years, as Rukhadze explains, iFact’s financial situation is far from unique. Batumelebi and Netgazeti are also struggling financially: “It’s not about a bright future or expansion or professional growth or anything. It’s about just survival,” Rukhadze stresses. 

In March 2026, access to foreign funding was further restricted when the Georgian parliament adopted new amendments to the law on grants, expanding the definition of a “grant.” In 2023, the ruling Georgian Dream government tried to adopt legislation requiring media and civil society organizations that receive over 20 percent of their funding from abroad to register as “foreign agents.”

Although mass protests prevented its immediate adoption, the “Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence,” commonly known as the “Russian law” due to its perceived similarity to Russia’s “foreign agent” law, was passed in May 2024. Batumelebi and Netgazeti have refused to register as foreign agents, Rukhadze tells us, as have most Georgian independent media.

Amid such restricted legal and political circumstances, the trust between sources and journalists has been disrupted. Georgians are now often reluctant to talk to iFact’s journalists and request to speak under anonymity in fear of consequences, explains Bakradze. There have been cases of people who have lost their jobs or access to social aid after openly criticizing the government, she adds. 

Attacks, smear campaigns, and surveillance

Since 2023, watchdogs have recorded 65 cases of physical assault and 83 verbal attacks against Georgian reporters.

Sulkhan Meskhidze, who started working as a journalist in 2010, is no stranger to physical and verbal harassment. Such incidents have intensified in the last five years, he tells iMEdD, highlighting that in nearly half of his in-the-field reporting trips, he becomes the target of attacks.

The most serious attack Meskhidze faced came in February 2025, while he was reporting on the deaths of two kids at a public construction site in an area of Batumi called “Dream City.” A group of people began throwing stones at him and demanding that he leave. According to Meskhidze, the aggressors were local residents and government supporters.

The police were present, Meskhidze says, but did nothing to protect him. Even when he managed to record and publish evidence of such attacks, authorities still remained indifferent. 

iFact has recently experienced a different type of attack, in the form of smear campaigns. After the outlet published an investigation regarding how Russian oil continues to move through Georgian ports despite international sanctions, the European Commission decided to put Georgia’s Kulevi port on a potential sanctions list. Following that, in March 2026, pro-government media “labeled us as spies of the British intelligence service,” Bakradze explains.

Physical and digital surveillance presents another challenge for iFact. “A lot of the time we see the state security people around us,” Bakradze says. Their phones are also being surveilled and cyberattacks are common.

Survival tactics: From wine tasting to yoga

Bakradze, who co-founded iFact in 2016, tells iMEdD she would not have decided to establish an outlet today.

When you start the week on Monday, you never know if you’ll last until Friday or not.

Since losing their foreign grant revenue, iFact is now relying entirely on local Georgian-derived income, selling a monthly newsletter on sanctions evasion, while also offering a paid membership, the first outlet in Georgia to do so, she says. Events are another revenue source, with iFact organizing a wine tasting event in May 2026.

What has helped iFact’s reporters cope with stress is making themselves busy and seeing the results of their investigations, Bakradze says, adding that “we do yoga as a team.” Sulkhan Meskhidze worries mostly about the stress his family is facing, who live in constant fear for his wellbeing.

“The lights must stay on”

Georgia’s independent media have forged a collective response in the form of Sinatle Media, a solidarity and sustainability network of 22 online media. As Sinatle’s Chair of the Board and journalist at the investigative outlet Studio Monitor, Teo Kavtaradze tells iMEdD, the need for a united front became increasingly urgent in April 2025, after the law requiring government approval to obtain foreign grants was adopted. Following a lengthy bureaucratic process, Sinatle Media was born in July 2025. The Georgian journalists who spoke to iMEdD all work for media outlets that belong to the network.

In Georgian, Sinatle means “light.” Both the name and the network’s slogan, “The lights must stay on,” were chosen to underscore a shared conviction: “If the lights go out, the truth disappears with them,” Kavtaradze highlights.

One of Sinatle Media’s main functions involves collecting funds that are allocated to its 22 members. Through a series of events, including book fairs, flea markets, and artwork auctions, Sinatle has managed to raise GEL 260,000 (approximately EUR 84,000).

The network also provides cost-sharing services, which proved particularly valuable in December 2025 during a smear campaign against the network. Sinatle Media helped its members secure legal support to counter these allegations.

One of Sinatle’s main achievements, according to Kavtaradze, is that this is “the first case when we [Georgian media] are actually helping each other […] and we are building this solidarity together.”

Written by Incubator for Media Education and Development (iMEdD)

item.title: Riddims against copyright
item.dc:creator: Global Voices Caribbean
item.description: Dancehall’s interactive, collaborative nature doesn’t treat a work as isolated or even something that is “finished.” Iteration is a part of the creative process that is decided by the next function or party.
item.content:encoded:
The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage, and copyright law is no exception

Originally published on Global Voices

Copyright chaser from eff.org. Fair use.

By Alexis Hancock

“Oh! Bob Marley, right?” Jamaican culture has been popularised by the mainstream, and as a Jamaican-American, I often get a glimpse into how others have consumed it and from what point of view. I would not call myself an ardent Marley fan, but I know the kind of people who are most likely attached to his music outside of Jamaica — for example, the potential counterculture student of the 1970s at UCLA who found connection to his messages of resistance. 

My personal fascination with Jamaican music is the “riddim” — the Jamaican patois spelling of “rhythm” — an instrumental beat or tune constructed not for a single artist, but to be used by the collective of the time and to be both enjoyed and critiqued by the culture makers of Jamaican art: the disenfranchised masses. 

As a public interest technologist and digital rights advocate, I view the “riddim” with an open-source lens. It helped to protect Jamaican culture, particularly from Western constructs that are heavily embedded in existing power dynamics like rigid copyright laws and the corporate commodification of music.

Riddims

Dancehall’s interactive, collaborative nature doesn’t treat a work as isolated or even something that is “finished.” Iteration is a part of the creative process that is decided by the next function or party. In Larisa Kingston Mann’s “Rude Citizenship,” she outlines how copyright law was written at a time when many of the island’s people were themselves considered property under slavery, thereby creating — from the very start — a contentious relationship with those holding the society’s wealth. Copyright law was set up for those with ample resources to dictate what could be protected and who could profit.

Beat-sharing directly challenges neo-colonial copyright’s individualistic definition of ownership and originality. Traditional copyright promotes monopoly over expression, enforced by harsh legal mechanisms (such as statutory damages) that make intertextuality, reuse, and artistic experimentation legally risky. Even Sean Paul, one of the most commercially successful dancehall artists in the world, attributed his mainstream success of “Get Busy” to the Diwali Riddim. If not for this collective creativity and shared use, we would not see dancehall music evolve and get pushed to the world in the way that it has.

Collective sharing didn’t stop at just music; dance was often learned collectively as well. I used to watch “passa passa” videos in high school and college, just to learn and keep up to date with the latest dances coming out of Jamaica and New York City in the early 2000s. These parties were the bane of anyone entrenched in respectability. The clothes were outlandish, the manners “rude,” the dancehall queens nothing short of acrobatic, and the parties could go until 6:00 a.m. 

But this was also the time when new artists could get a slot, vendors could make a little money, and producers could collaborate with artists and get public consensus on what worked before dropping money at a studio.

Caribbean economics

Library of Congress – Banana farming in Jamaica. Fair use.

The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage in many ways, and copyright law is no exception.

Jamaica was often sidelined into less than favourable international trade agreements that didn’t keep the interests of the Jamaican masses in mind. More often than not, there was a strict one-size-fits-all structure, dictated by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank: detrimental loan structures, one-sided economic trade agreements, currency devaluation, and exploitative labour guidelines. 

In 1992, the IMF created terms that heavily impacted Jamaica’s economy. This served as the backdrop for the Jamaica Copyright Act of 1993, when the country was directed to reshape its laws to participate in global trade. More rigid terms forced artists to start registering “riddims,” and while these laws are purported to protect artists, less resourced and independent artists struggled to make claims against large producers. This also killed the “handshake agreements” many artists and producers made prior to 1993.

Modern dancehall and beyond

This hasn’t stopped dancehall creators from organising alternative circuits of commerce and performance, social intimacy, and communal engagement. Even today, the continuous nature of dancehall works still causes friction with how copyright laws function. 

This year, a monumental copyright case was overturned by a U.S. federal judge who named many famous artists in a list of 150, and affected about 2,000 tracks. The plaintiffs, Cleveland “Clevie” Browne and the heirs of Wycliffe “Steely” Johnson, claimed that the “Fish Market” riddim (also known as the “Pocoman Jam riddim”) was the basis and source of the percussion pattern that runs through reggaeton, the now billion-dollar musical genre with origins in the Spanish reggae of Panama brought by  Afro-Jamaican migrants, and further magnified by Puerto Rican artists.

However, the logic was denied. As US District Judge André Birotte Jr. said, “Plaintiffs have not clearly identified what copyrighted work contains the allegedly protectable selection and arrangement they seek to enforce.”

The claim failed to take all selections and arrangements mentioned and tie them to one work. But rather, it referenced a collection of works that mirrored parts over time: “That principle is especially significant here. Skidmore cautioned that a plaintiff cannot ‘reconstitut[e] the copyrighted work as a combination of unprotectable elements’ and then claim that those elements are substantially similar because they appear in an accused work, even where the elements are presented in ‘a different aesthetic context.’”

The nature of riddims is a double-edged sword here. Browne and Johnson were deprived of a chance to share in the profits of their creativity that set the groundwork for a whole new genre of music. If this lawsuit had gone in their favour, the logic could potentially have put any new reggaeton artist to this profit-sharing standard, possibly resulting in conditions only well-backed artists like Bad Bunny could afford to accommodate. Such an outcome could have created a disempowering dynamic for new artists. A power structure riddims fought in the first place.

We can all easily hear the main percussion in Puerto Rican reggaeton and Dominican dembow, but copyright’s ears are selectively biased against rhythm — usually favouring money, the artist’s will to attribute credit to where it’s due, and when the tracks were created in the more popular artist’s career. In fact, Black artists are often credited much later for genre-defining work and after lighter-skinned artists have made their money.

Despite the mainstream push away from collective processes, dancehall continues to evolve. What “makes Jamaicans cool” is the layers of understanding that come with what we share. Copyright creates a stamp in time — a piece of “the cool” the mainstream can manage to freeze and sell. Yet, the true cool develops alongside the collective and remains protected by that shared understanding.
